# Mahāhatthipadopama Sutta (MN 28 (PTS MN i 184))

**ID:** MN 28 (PTS MN i 184)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Mahāhatthipadopama Sutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Longer Simile of the Elephant’s Footprint
**PTS:** MN i 184
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/mn28
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0201m.mul2.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mahāhatthipadopama Sutta* ("The Longer Simile of the Elephant’s Footprint", MN 28) is the twenty-eighth discourse in the *Majjhimanikāya* [Buswell & Lopez 2014; SuttaCentral]. Delivered by the Venerable Sāriputta, its governing pedagogical framework is the simile that just as the footprints of all living beings fit within that of an elephant, so all wholesome states and teachings are subsumed under the Four Noble Truths [Buswell & Lopez 2014; Nyanaponika et al. 2003; SuttaCentral]. Sāriputta develops this by examining the truth of suffering in terms of the five aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*), focusing extensively on material form (*rūpa*) divided into the four primary elements (*mahābhūta*): earth, water, fire, and wind [Buswell & Lopez 2014; Nyanaponika et al. 2003; Radich 2007]. Each element is contemplated across its internal (bodily) and external manifestations, demonstrating their impermanence and insubstantiality to cultivate non-attachment and eliminate self-identification [Radich 2007; Segall 2003; Wen, Sukkhavipassaka]. The text also preserves the well-known dictum that seeing dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) is equivalent to seeing the Dhamma [IABU 2012; Radich 2007].

MN 28 has a direct Chinese parallel in the *Madhyama-āgama* (MĀ 30, *Xiangjiyu jing* 象跡喩經), which provides explicit definitions for all four elements, whereas the Pali text presents the detailed characteristic formula only for the earth element [Buswell & Lopez 2014; Meisig 2010; SuttaCentral; Wen, Sukkhavipassaka]. SuttaCentral also marks MN 21 (*Kakacūpama Sutta*) as a full parallel and notes a citation in the *Kathāvatthu* (Kv 22.8) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus records dense Pali-internal text reuse with element and aggregate expositions, particularly in the *Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta* (MN 140) and *Mahārāhulovāda Sutta* (MN 62), alongside extensive shared segments across the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* (AN 4, AN 7), *Saṁyutta Nikāya* (SN 22, SN 35), and the *Vibhaṅga* (Vb 3) [DharmaNexus; Wen, Sukkhavipassaka]. Furthermore, DharmaNexus detects cross-language alignments with Sanskrit works including Śāntideva's *Śikṣāsamuccaya* and the *Śrāvakabhūmi*, as well as Tibetan canonical sūtras [DharmaNexus]. The sutta is commented upon in the *Majjhimanikāya-aṭṭhakathā* and referenced in the *Visuddhimagga* regarding elemental analysis [DharmaNexus; Wen, Sukkhavipassaka]. Notable English translations include those by I. B. Horner, Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli and Bhikkhu Bodhi, and Bhikkhu Sujato [Berkwitz 2013; SuttaCentral].

- [Berkwitz 2013] Stephen C. Berkwitz, Buddhist Poetry and Colonialism: Alagiyavanna and the Portuguese in Sri Lanka (2013) — References to psychic and physical elements in MN 28 and translation by Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi.
- [Segall 2003] Seth Robert Segall (ed.), Encountering Buddhism: Western Psychology and Buddhist Teachings (2003) — Glossary summary of MN 28 on materiality and nonself, and role in explaining aggregates.
